title: Too Many Neurons: Naturally Occurring Cell Death

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: How can overproduction followed by target-dependent survival match a developing neuron population to its target?
cards.back: More neurons are made than will survive. Limited support from the target keeps some alive; changing that support changes how many remain.
cards.quote: Make too many, then let the target keep what it can support.

cards.front: For a neuron, its {{c1::target}} is the tissue its axon grows to and connects with.
cards.back: For a limb motor neuron, the target is muscle.
cards.quote: A target is the tissue an axon grows to and connects with, here the muscles of a limb.

cards.front: Where are the cell bodies of the chick motor neurons that serve one leg grouped?
cards.back: In the lateral motor column of the lumbosacral spinal cord.
cards.quote: the column for the leg lies in the lumbosacral segments, in the lower back.

cards.front: Why does a low final neuron count after target removal fail to establish increased cell death?
cards.back: Fewer neurons could have been made, arrived at the counted site, or acquired the counted identity; alternatively, neurons could have formed and died.
cards.quote: a count made only at the end cannot tell them apart.

cards.front: After removing a developing neuron population’s target, how would you distinguish reduced production from later death using counts over time?
cards.back: Count healthy and dying neurons in matched regions of operated and control embryos at closely spaced stages. Equal early counts followed by excess dying cells and a deficit support later death.
cards.quote: In each embryo, count two things on both sides, in the same spinal segments: healthy neurons and dying ones.

cards.front: Why can sparse observations miss substantial developmental neuron death?
cards.back: Dying cells are cleared quickly, so few may be visible at one time. Closely spaced samples are needed to catch a death wave.
cards.quote: Dying cells are cleared fast, so a missing burst of them means something only if you sampled often enough to catch it.

cards.front: A neuron’s birth date is the time of its precursor’s {{c1::last division}}.
cards.back: Birthdating identifies when the neuron was made.
cards.quote: a neuron's birth date is the time of the last division of the precursor that made it.

cards.front: Healthy-neuron counts fall behind controls after target removal, but reduced production remains possible. What additional measurement would test whether normal numbers were initially made?
cards.back: Birthdate the neurons and compare the labelled cohorts in operated and control regions. Normal initial labelled numbers support formation of the cohort before its later loss.
cards.quote: Then confirm that labelled motor neurons were made in normal numbers on both sides.

cards.front: How did the 1949 study of chick spinal ganglia challenge the view that the limb mainly makes sensory neurons form?
cards.back: Many sensory neurons formed and extended fibres before the deficit; degeneration and clearance became conspicuous later. This supported a main role in survival.
cards.quote: Many neurons formed and sent out fibres before the deficit appeared;

cards.front: What does a pyknotic nucleus look like in a dying neuron?
cards.back: Small, dark and condensed, because its chromatin has collapsed.
cards.quote: Its chromatin collapses into a small, dark, condensed nucleus, a pyknotic nucleus.

cards.front: In normal chick embryos, when does most lumbar lateral motor-column neuron loss occur, and what approximate raw counts bracket it?
cards.back: Most loss occurs during incubation days 6.5–9.5, between a peak just over 20,000 and a plateau about 12,000.
cards.quote: Most of the loss came between days 6.5 and 9.5.

cards.front: Use the approximate chick lumbar motor-neuron counts of 20,000 at the peak and 12,000 later. With no new neurons joining, what fraction of the peak population was lost?
cards.back: Loss ≈ 20,000 − 12,000 = 8,000 neurons. Fraction lost ≈ 8,000/20,000 = 0.40, or 40%. Use the peak population as the denominator.
cards.quote: Divide by the peak, the number that was there to lose.

cards.front: Why are Hamburger’s absolute lumbar motor-neuron counts approximate even though the roughly 40% loss is robust?
cards.back: A nucleus crossing neighbouring sections can be counted twice. Corrected counts lower both the peak and plateau but still indicate about 40% loss.
cards.quote: These are raw counts: a nucleus cut across two neighbouring sections can be counted twice.

cards.front: Extra target tissue is added to a developing motor-neuron population. Assuming other processes stay unchanged, what early-versus-late count pattern would distinguish increased production from improved survival?
cards.back: Increased production gives a larger count before the death period. Improved survival gives equal starting counts, then more survivors on the treated side during the death period.
cards.quote: Fewer deaths, equal cohorts at the start: the two sides are equal at day 6,

cards.front: What did Hollyday and Hamburger’s extra-leg graft show about chick motor-neuron survival?
cards.back: Counts matched at day 6 but were about 11%–28% higher later with vigorously moving grafts, supporting fewer deaths among neurons already present.
cards.quote: So the extra leg did not detectably add neurons by day 6; the later difference fits fewer deaths among the neurons already present.

cards.front: Why did the chick extra-leg experiment leave open whether targets can influence neuron production earlier in development?
cards.back: The graft was added around the time these neurons were being born. It therefore tested little about target effects before that stage.
cards.quote: The graft went in around the time these neurons were being born,

cards.front: Why describe the limiting target contribution in the chick extra-leg experiment as “support” rather than a proven specific trophic signal?
cards.back: The experiment left open whether the limiting resource was synaptic space or a trophic agent; it did not identify a particular survival molecule.
cards.quote: Hollyday and Hamburger left open whether that something was synaptic space or a trophic agent,

cards.front: For a chick lumbar motor column with about 20,000 neurons at its peak and 12,000 normal survivors, calculate the greatest percentage increase in survivors if no neurons join after the peak.
cards.back: At most about 20,000 survive. Maximum increase ≈ (20,000 − 12,000)/12,000 × 100 = 66.7%, or about 67%, relative to normal survivors.
cards.quote: Only about 20,000 were present at the peak.

cards.front: A target-enlargement experiment starts with the same measured peak neuron count as its control, yet later survivors exceed that peak. How would you investigate the apparent violation of rescue-only survival?
cards.back: Rescue alone cannot exceed the starting cohort if no neurons join. Count across time, birthdate new cells, and trace lineages to test later additions or changes in counted identity.
cards.quote: So the target turns a dial: more target, fewer deaths, up to a ceiling set by the neurons present.

cards.front: A researcher applies the extra-leg study’s percentage gains to normal counts from a separate study and calls the resulting survivor totals direct measurements. How should that claim be corrected?
cards.back: They illustrate scale, rather than measure those grafts. The percentages and baseline counts come from different experiments.
cards.quote: which come from different experiments, so treat it as an illustration of scale, not a measurement.

cards.front: Most developing neurons that die undergo {{c1::apoptosis}}, a programmed process run by the cell’s own machinery.
cards.back: Bcl-2 family proteins and caspases participate in that machinery.
cards.quote: Most developing neurons die by apoptosis instead, a programmed death run by the cell's own machinery

cards.front: An apoptotic neuron exposes {{c1::phosphatidylserine}} on its outer membrane face as an engulfment signal.
cards.back: This lipid is normally kept on the inner face.
cards.quote: It also flips phosphatidylserine, a lipid normally kept on the inner face of the membrane, to the outside.

cards.front: Which resident phagocytes clear dying neurons in the brain and spinal cord?
cards.back: Microglia.
cards.quote: microglia, the resident phagocytes, in the brain and spinal cord,

cards.front: How does the appearance of typical injury-related necrosis differ from neuronal apoptosis?
cards.back: Necrosis typically involves swelling, bursting and inflammation. Apoptosis involves chromatin condensation, cell shrinkage and fragmentation followed by engulfment.
cards.quote: Necrosis is typically death from injury: the cell swells, bursts and spills its contents, and the tissue becomes inflamed.

cards.front: Why is “half of all neurons die” an unreliable rule for vertebrate development?
cards.back: Counted populations lose about a fifth to four-fifths within defined developmental windows. The fraction depends on the population; these observations do not describe adult loss.
cards.quote: In the populations that have been counted, between about a fifth and four-fifths of the neurons die, depending on the population.

cards.front: In the developing rat retina, about {{c1::half}} of the retinal ganglion cells are eliminated.
cards.back: The fraction belongs to this population, rather than to all developing neurons.
cards.quote: In the rat retina, about half of the ganglion cells,

cards.front: In mouse cortical interneurons, about {{c1::40%}} die after birth.
cards.back: This is a population-specific developmental loss.
cards.quote: in mouse cortical interneurons about 40% die after birth.

cards.front: What two functions can overproduction followed by developmental neuron death serve?
cards.back: Matching neuron number to available target support, and preferentially eliminating neurons with incorrect or weak connections.
cards.quote: If survival depends on support received at the right target, neurons that went wrong can lose out.
cards.section: Why make neurons just to kill them?

cards.front: Curare blocks transmission from nerve to muscle in chick embryos. During the later, target-dependent death period, what happens to motor-neuron survival, and what does that result establish?
cards.back: Many neurons otherwise destined to die survive. This shows that events at the muscle affect survival; it does not establish selective elimination of wrong connections.
cards.quote: That shows survival depends on what happens at the muscle, not that death picks out wrong connections.
cards.section: Why make neurons just to kill them?

cards.front: A developing neuron has a mistargeted axon branch. Must correcting this error involve neuron death, and why?
cards.back: No. Pruning an axon branch can correct wiring while the neuron survives; eliminating whole neurons is only one route to correcting connections.
cards.quote: Many wiring errors are corrected by pruning axon branches or synapses,
cards.section: Why make neurons just to kill them?

cards.front: What did transplantation of chick cervical neural tube to another segmental level show about the early motor-neuron death wave?
cards.back: The early death schedule persisted, supporting timing carried within the transplanted tube. This did not locate the schedule in individual neurons rather than their neighbours.
cards.quote: Cervical neural tube transplanted to other segmental levels kept its early death, so the schedule was carried within that tube.

cards.front: In chick early cervical motor-neuron death, target enlargement fails to alter loss, but blocking RNA or protein synthesis reduces it. What mechanism is supported?
cards.back: An active death program requiring new RNA and protein is supported. The tested target enlargement does not control this early wave.
cards.quote: Drugs that block RNA or protein synthesis reduced it, so it needs new RNA and protein, an active program.

cards.front: In a hypothetical graft model, a host supports exactly 1,000 cells and no other process kills them. What fraction dies when the dose rises from 1,000 to 5,000 cells?
cards.back: At 1,000 cells: (1,000 − 1,000)/1,000 = 0%. At 5,000: (5,000 − 1,000)/5,000 = 80%. Survivors equal the smaller of dose and capacity.
cards.quote: Survivors are the smaller of the dose and 1,000.

cards.front: Why do dose and timing results from mouse cortical interneuron grafts answer different questions about developmental death?
cards.back: An unchanged dying fraction across doses argues against a fixed host survival supply. Death at donor-cell age supports a carried schedule. The timing rule alone does not predict the fraction lost.
cards.quote: These are separate results: timing by itself does not tell you what fraction dies.

cards.front: Chick cervical neural tube retains its death schedule after transplantation. Would this result prove an independent clock in each neuron? Explain the remaining alternative.
cards.back: No. The rule supported is that timing travels with the tube. Neighbouring cells travel too and could carry the schedule; the graft does not separate those possibilities.
cards.quote: Whether it was carried by each doomed neuron or by its neighbours, the grafts could not say.

cards.front: A developing neuron population loses its usual marker, but no dying cells are seen in sparse samples. What tracing strategy could distinguish movement or identity change from cell loss?
cards.back: Use a permanent lineage label to find descendants elsewhere or with another marker, and sample death frequently enough to detect rapidly cleared corpses.
cards.quote: Counting across time, tracing the cells, and changing the target or the number of cells help narrow down which one happened.

cards.front: Precursors from younger and older donors are grafted into hosts of one age. Death follows donor-cell age rather than host age. What does this establish about timing?
cards.back: The schedule travels with the transplanted cells rather than following host age. This result alone does not establish what sets the fraction that dies.
cards.quote: Death timed by the donor cells' age, not the host's, points to a schedule carried by the cells.

cards.front: A newly studied hindbrain population declines during development. Design a test of whether target size controls survival rather than initial production or cell identity.
cards.back: Count healthy and dying cells frequently; birthdate and permanently label the cohort. Enlarge or reduce targets. The survival rule predicts equal early cohorts but target-dependent deaths and later counts, bounded by the peak count if no neurons join afterwards.
cards.quote: If the target sets survival, the counts match before the death period and diverge during it:

cards.front: A grafted neuron population dies at donor-cell age despite target manipulation. Why should a researcher still test local circuit activity when explaining how many survive?
cards.back: Timing and fraction are separate controls. The stated interneuron rule allows a carried death schedule while local circuit activity can tune survival; target-insensitive timing cannot establish a fixed dying fraction.
cards.quote: A cell-carried schedule does not rule out tuning by the surrounding circuit, as in the cortical interneurons.

cards.front: In newborn rat retina, tetrodotoxin prevents preferential loss of mistargeted ganglion cells while total deaths remain about unchanged. What does comparing these readouts reveal?
cards.back: Activity affects which neurons die without necessarily changing how many. The rule is to distinguish selective error correction from overall population matching; total deaths alone would miss the loss of selection.
cards.quote: stops the preferential loss of cells with mistargeted axons, though about the same total number still die.
cards.section: Error correction in the rat retina

cards.front: What does continued developmental neuron loss in mice lacking caspase-3 or caspase-9 show about using apoptotic appearance as the sole death measure?
cards.back: Death can continue more slowly without the apoptotic look. Absence of that appearance does not establish survival; apoptosis is not the only route.
cards.quote: about the same number of developing neurons still die, more slowly and without the apoptotic look.
